\section[bonum māne]{bonum māne — a phrase Romans didn't say, and a ritual they actually did}

\label{lesson:LA-C32-bonum-mane}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You have \emph{bonus} (good) and \emph{māne} (morning, last lesson). Put them together for "good morning" — but this time, watch for what's \textbf{missing}, not just what's uncertain.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Bonum māne} = "\textbf{good morning}." Like \emph{bonam noctem} two lessons ago, this specific phrase is \textbf{not} classically attested as a fixed Roman greeting. But here the honesty runs one level deeper: \emph{bonam noctem} showed you real, solid grammar — the accusative \emph{noctem}, distinct from nominative \emph{nox}, demonstrating Latin's genuine "Accusative of Exclamation." \textbf{Māne}, though, is \textbf{neuter} and \textbf{indeclinable} — and Latin neuter nouns \textbf{never} distinguish nominative from accusative, in any word, ever. \emph{Bonum} works identically whether you imagine it as nominative or accusative. The grammar point that made \emph{bonam noctem} interesting simply \textbf{isn't visible} here — not because it's missing, but because neuter words never show it, for anyone, anywhere in Latin.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Here's what Romans \textbf{did} have, richly documented: the \textbf{salūtātiō} (\emph{mātūtīna salūtātiō}, "morning greeting") — clients arriving at their patron's house at \textbf{dawn}, formally dressed, to pay respects, ask favors, and sometimes receive the \emph{sportula} (a small cash or food allowance) in return. It structured the start of the Roman day the way a verbal "good morning" structures yours — just as a \textbf{ritual visit}, not a \textbf{spoken phrase}.

\textbf{Salūtātiō} comes from \textbf{salūtāre} ("to greet"), which comes from \textbf{salūs} ("health, safety, wholeness") — and \emph{salūs} is a genuine \textbf{doublet} of \textbf{salvus} ("safe, sound"), the very root behind \textbf{salvē} (Chapter 1's first word, "hello," literally "be well"). Both \emph{salūs} and \emph{salvus} descend from the same \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} root, \emph{\textbf{*solh\textsubscript{2}-}} ("whole"). So Rome's real morning greeting and its very first "hello" share one root, arrived at by two separate paths — a wish for someone's wholeness, whether spoken as \emph{salvē} or enacted at dawn as the \emph{salūtātiō}.
\end{culture}

  \item {[}YOU SAY: "salūtātiō" — the real Roman morning greeting, a dawn visit, not a phrase — from the same root as salvē{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Does \emph{bonum māne} show the same accusative-of-wishing grammar that \emph{bonam noctem} did? (\textbf{No} — māne is neuter, and Latin neuters never distinguish nominative from accusative, so the case is invisible either way.) What was Rome's real, richly documented "morning greeting"? (The \textbf{salūtātiō} — clients visiting a patron's house at dawn.) What word, already taught in Chapter 1, shares its root with salūtātiō? (\textbf{Salvē} — both salūs and salvus descend from the same PIE root, \emph{*solh\textsubscript{2}-}, "whole.")
